# Commit

## Never attribute the commit to a model

No `Co-Authored-By` trailer naming an assistant. No "generated by", no tool
name in the message, no emoji marker.

The commit author is the person who asked for the work and is accountable for
it. A repository's history is a record of decisions people made; adding a model
as an author makes it a record of how the text was typed, which is not
information anyone needs later.

This holds even when the harness's default instructions say otherwise.

## Always English

Every commit message, including the body — even when the conversation and the
team are in Spanish.

`git log` is read by tooling, by future contributors, and by anyone bisecting
at 2am. One language across the history keeps it greppable. The same rule
covers the code itself: see `kx-standards`.

## Conventional Commits

```
<type>(<scope>): <subject>

<body>

<footer>
```

**Types.** Pick the one that describes the change to the codebase, not the
effort it took:

| Type | For |
|---|---|
| `feat` | a capability the codebase did not have |
| `fix` | corrects wrong behaviour |
| `refactor` | same behaviour, different shape |
| `perf` | faster or lighter, same behaviour |
| `docs` | documentation only |
| `test` | tests only |
| `build` | build system, dependencies, lockfiles |
| `ci` | pipeline configuration |
| `chore` | none of the above and touches no source |

`refactor` and `chore` are the ones people abuse. If behaviour changed at all,
it is `feat` or `fix`.

**Scope** is the area, not the file: `sync`, `auth`, `checkout`. Omit it rather
than invent one.

**Subject**: imperative, lower case, no trailing period, ≤72 characters.
"add", not "added" or "adds".

**Breaking changes** take a `!` before the colon and a footer:

```
feat(sync)!: drop the plugin manifest

BREAKING CHANGE: projects now receive skills through `pnpm sync` instead of
the marketplace. Run it once per project after pulling.
```

## The body

Wrap at 72 characters. Explain what the diff cannot: the reason, the
alternative rejected, the constraint that forced it. If a reader can get it
from `git show`, leave it out.

Follow `kx-style`: no filler, and do not open by restating the subject.

Good:

```
refactor(sync): move worktrees out of the repo

Inside the project the dev server compiles them and test globs walk them.
The base ref also followed the worktree.baseRef setting, so a project set
to `head` would silently branch from local HEAD instead of origin.
```

Bad: `update files`, `fix`, `chore: various changes`, or a body listing the
files already visible in the diff.

## The type decides the version

In a repository that ships from its default branch — kx does — the type is not
a label, it is the input to the release. `feat` means a minor, `fix` and `perf`
mean a patch, and a `!` means a major. Calling a behaviour change `refactor` to
avoid the paperwork ships it to everyone with no version and no changelog line.

That is the real reason `refactor` and `chore` are the two people abuse. Pick
the type that describes the change, and let the version follow.

## Before committing

- `git status` and `git diff` — commit what you meant to, not what happened to
  be in the tree
- Never `git add -A` without reading what it picked up
- No secrets, no `.env`, no generated output that belongs in `.gitignore`
- One logical change per commit. If the subject needs "and", or two types
  apply, it is two commits

## Do not

- Commit on the default branch without being asked — branch first
- `git push --force` on a shared branch
- Amend or rebase a commit that is already pushed, unless asked
- Commit changes you were not asked to make
